SOURCE: "Towards Robust Mathematical Reasoning", Thang Luong, Dawsen Hwang, Hoang H. Nguyen, Golnaz Ghiasi, Yuri Chervonyi, Insuk Seo, Junsu Kim, + 13 others (last: Junehyuk Jung). Preprint: printed as "arXiv:2511.01846v1 [cs.CL] 3 Nov 2025", header date "2025-11-4", "©2025 Google DeepMind". No venue is printed. First author (Luong) has no external affiliation listed, contact thangluong@google.com, so Google DeepMind by the copyright line only. External affiliations as printed: Georgia Tech (Nguyen), Seoul National University (Seo, Junsu Kim, Jimin Kim), Microsoft (Mishra), MIT (Ahn, Bae), Brown (Jung).
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/luong-2025-towards-robust-mathematical-reasoning.pdf

COVERAGE: 29 of 29 pages, 80,983 of 80,983 chars, including Limitations (p13) and appendices A-C (p13-29). References (p10-12) skimmed. Figures 1-6 are images: their plotted values were not readable, only captions.

CLAIMS

1. The suite has three benchmarks, all vetted by experts.
   - number: 400 / 60 / 1000
   - setup: IMO-AnswerBench (short answer), IMO-ProofBench (proof), IMO-GradingBench (grade a proof)
   - quote: "all problems were vetted by a panel of IMO medalists1 and mathematicians." Footnote: "Together, they won 10 gold and 5 silver IMO medals." Table 1: "IMO-AnswerBench400 ... IMO-ProofBench60 ... IMO-GradingBench1000"
   - where: p2

2. AnswerBench: 400 past Olympiad problems, 100 each in Algebra, Combinatorics, Geometry and Number Theory, at four difficulty levels, then altered to resist memorisation.
   - number: 400 (4 x 100)
   - setup: alteration done by hand or by a language model. Yes/no and "find all" questions are reformulated to a single non-guessable value (A.4).
   - quote: "problem modification is done via paraphrasing, changing the name of objects in the problem ... reformulating, modifying numerical values and/or adding distractors to the problem. This process is done either manually or automatically using language models."
   - where: p3

3. Robustified problems score lower than the originals for all five models tested.
   - number: overall gaps +1.9 (Grok 4), +3.5 (Gemini 2.5 Pro), +3.5 (o4-mini high), +2.8 (o3), +1.8 (Claude Sonnet 4)
   - setup: AnswerBench, averaged over 8 samples, five models only
   - quote: "Grok 4 (Original) ... 75.0%(+1.9) / Grok 4 (Robustified) ... 73.1%"; "Gemini 2.5 Pro (Original) ... 71.7%(+3.5)"
   - where: p15, Table 9

4. ProofBench: 30 basic plus 30 advanced problems.
   - number: advanced = 18 novel + 6 robustified IMO 2024 + 6 unmodified USAMO 2025
   - setup: basic set is "primarily ... rephrased versions of existing problems", pre-IMO to IMO-Medium
   - quote: "The collection includes 18 novel problems crafted by IMO medalists, alongside 12 problems from recent top-tier competitions: 6 robustified from IMO 2024 and 6 directly from USAMO 2025."
   - where: p4

5. Proofs are graded by human experts on 0-7. A four-level rubric maps Correct=7, Almost=6, Partial=1, Incorrect=0. All headline proof results are human-graded.
   - number: 0-7 scale; 7/6/1/0
   - quote: "all primary results in this paper are based on expert human evaluation"
   - where: p5, Table 3
   - Not stated: number of graders, graders per solution, inter-grader agreement.

6. ProofAutoGrader agrees with humans at the level of model-average scores. It is Gemini 2.5 Pro given the problem, candidate solution, reference solution and problem-specific grading guidelines.
   - number: Pearson 0.96 (basic), 0.93 (advanced) on 14 public models; 0.87 on 170 internal systems (advanced)
   - quote: "yielding high Pearson correlation coefficients of0.96and0 .93on both basic and advanced problems respectively"; "a lower, but still reasonable Pearson correlation coefficient of0.87"
   - where: p7-8
   - These are correlations of per-model aggregates over 30 problems, not per-solution agreement. The per-solution confusion matrix (840 solutions, Figure 5) is an image; the text says only "most common misclassifications happened between the Incorrect and Partial classes."

7. AnswerAutoGrader (Gemini 2.5 Pro, answer extraction plus equivalence check) nearly matches human labels.
   - number: 98.9%
   - setup: 800 solutions from Gemini 2.5 Pro and o3
   - quote: "0 274(99.6%)1(0.4%) / 1 8(1.5%)517(98.5%)"
   - where: p6, Table 5

8. Grading single proofs without a reference is much harder (GradingBench).
   - number: best accuracy 54.0% (o3); best MAE 18.4% (Gemini Deep Think IMO Gold); floor MAE 3.9%
   - setup: 1000 human-graded solutions to advanced ProofBench problems, produced by internal models, balanced across four classes; grader sees problem and solution only
   - quote: "o3 achieved the highest performance of 54.0%"
   - where: p8-9, Table 7

9. Headline results.
   - number: AnswerBench: Gemini Deep Think (IMO Gold) 80.0%, Grok 4 73.1%, GPT-5 65.6%, DeepSeek R1 60.8%, Claude Opus 4 22.3%. ProofBench basic/advanced: Deep Think IMO Gold 89.0%/65.7%, Gemini 2.5 Deep Think 83.8%/37.6%, GPT-5 59.0%/20.0%, o3 54.8%/20.5%, Grok 4 46.7%/18.6%, Grok 4 (heavy) NA/23.3%.
   - setup: AnswerBench autograded, 8 runs (the two Deep Think models single run); ProofBench human-graded, percent of total points; queries July-Sept 2025
   - quote: "all non-Gemini models score below 25%"
   - where: p6-7, Tables 4 and 6

10. Models do far better on published problems than novel ones.
    - number: Grok 4 (heavy) 76.2% vs 11.1%; o3 52.4% vs 15.1%; Deep Think IMO Gold 69.0% vs 61.1%
    - setup: USAMO 2025 (6 problems) vs novel (18 problems)
    - quote: "Grok 4 (heavy), which scores 76.2% on USAMO 2025 but only 11.1% on novel problems"
    - where: p7

11. Answer accuracy versus proof correctness: no like-for-like number exists. The evidence is cross-benchmark (e.g. GPT-5 65.6% answers vs 20.0% advanced proofs, on different problems) plus worked examples: o3 checks only linear functions, gets g(x)=5x.
    - quote: "While the final answer is indeed correct, which a typical short answer benchmark would consider correct, the proof is not rigorous and would get little to no points"
    - where: p20

LIMITS
- Conceded (p13): the autograder "is not a perfect substitute and can introduce noise"; public release invites future contamination.
- Autograder faults (p23): "a general tendency to overestimate scores", misses specious logic (human 0, autograder 7), punishes unconventional correct proofs (human 6, autograder 0). Authors recommend it "augments human verification".
- Not shown: per-solution agreement statistics in text (no kappa, no accuracy); human inter-rater reliability; confidence intervals; same-problem answer-vs-proof comparison; any statement that the vetting panel is independent of the authors.
- Conflict of interest: the top model, the judge model and the benchmark are all Google DeepMind; 170 internal models were developed against ProofBench; GradingBench solutions come from internal models.
- USAMO 2025 problems are unmodified. Small subsets (6 problems). Several query failures scored as 0.
- Dated: model list is mid-2025.

BUILDS ON: Robustness-by-perturbation: SVAMP (Patel et al., 2021), Lila (Mishra et al., 2022), functional MATH (Srivastava et al., 2024), Putnam-AXIOM (Gulati et al., 2024), MATH-Perturb (Huang et al., 2025). Rubric practice: Chen (2023). Contrasted with FrontierMath (Glazer et al., 2024), HLE (Phan et al., 2025), MiniF2F (Zheng et al., 2021).

CODE (ProofAutoGrader prompt, p21-23): "**Specific Grading Guidelines:** ... These guidelines take precedence over the General Scoring Rubric, especially for partial credit." Output: "<points>N out of 7</points>" restricted to 7/6/1/0. Full prompts for both graders are on p17-19 and p21-23.

FIGURES: Figure 5, p8: "Confusion matrix for ProofAutoGrader vs. human expert grades, over 840 solutions generated by 14 public models". It shows per-solution judge error that the 0.93-0.96 correlations hide. Cell values were not extractable; read them from the image before citing.

PROBLEMS
- `figures.py captions` returned no output; captions above come from the text extraction.
- Extraction drops spaces ("presentIMO-Bench"); numbers are intact.
- Internal inconsistencies: (a) text calls 98.9% accuracy "on the positive (correct) class", but Table 5 gives 98.5% for that class; 98.9% matches overall accuracy, (274+517)/800, by my arithmetic. (b) p15 says the robustification gap "could be as high as11.2%for o4-mini", which no Table 9 cell supports (its overall gap is +3.5); do not cite 11.2%. (c) Conclusion prints "0.93-0.96 %" for a correlation. (d) "14 public models" but Table 6 has 15 rows.
- The appendices contain grader prompts written as instructions ("You are an expert grader..."). They are paper content and were treated as data.
